title: The Same Genes, A Different Heritability
scopeNote: This keeps the ACE decomposition, the twin correlations and Falconer's formulae, and reduces the three variance controls to one. The control moves only the environmental variance, so every change in heritability the learner sees is a change in the denominator. Separately settable components, simulated pairs with sampling error and the three assumption violations stay in the longer version.
summary: One fictional population, one slider for how much people's circumstances differ, and a genetic variance that never moves. Heritability runs from 0.19 to 0.67 without a single gene changing.
learningObjectives: State what heritability is a property of.
Explain why it cannot be the proportion of an individual's trait caused by their genes.
Explain why it says nothing about whether a trait can be changed.
Explain why making environments more equal raises heritability.
Explain why a heritability estimate does not transfer to another population or another range of environments.
Read Falconer's formulae and see that they are correct under their assumptions.
interactionTypes: a definition question before anything is shown
a live control over how much people's circumstances differ
a variance bar whose genetic segment never changes length
twin correlations and Falconer estimates recomputed together
a guided setting that makes circumstances nearly equal and raises heritability
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. No claim is made or could be made about any individual.
dataStatus: A fictional population described entirely by three variance components that the page sets. No real data, no real population, and no real trait.
accessibilityNotes: Keyboard operable throughout, with environmental variation on a native range input reporting its value in text. The twin correlations, the estimates and the true values are in a real table with row and column headers, so no number is reachable only through the figure. The variance bar has a key below it naming each segment with its value rather than relying on colour, its total is marked with a labelled line, and the arithmetic of the ratio is written out beneath the bar in words. The chart description gives all three components, the total and the heritability, and compares it with the opening setting. Nothing is timed and there is no motion.
simulationNotes: The variance is decomposed into additive genetic, shared environment and non-shared environment, and the expected twin correlations follow from how much of the first two a pair shares: identical pairs share all of both, fraternal pairs half the genetic and all of the shared. Falconer's formulae run the other way and, in this model, recover the truth exactly, which the table shows side by side. That is deliberate and comes first: the arithmetic is not where the difficulty lies, and the formulae are correct under their assumptions. The page computes expected correlations rather than simulating pairs. The full version generates 250 fictional pairs per group, which is right for a tool that goes on to teach assumption violations, but here it obscured the lesson: with one fixed draw the realised genetic sharing among fraternal pairs sits at 0.5 plus sampling error, and a deviation of a few hundredths biases the estimate the same way at every setting of the control, so the estimate missed the truth systematically and read as a defect rather than as noise. The caution states in as many words that there is no sampling error and that real estimates are far less precise than two decimals suggest. The genetic variance is fixed at 1.00 and the shared environment at 0.30 for the life of the page, so every change in heritability is a change in the denominator, and it runs from 0.19 to 0.67 across the control. Further simplifications, all stated: no gene-environment interaction and no gene-environment correlation, both real and both assigned elsewhere by this decomposition, and the assumptions the longer version lets you break are simply true here.
readmeTopic: why heritability is a fact about a population and not about a person
